title: A Stray Page
summary: Your website lets visitors upload photos, and someone uploaded something that isn't a photo. Find it in the web log, read it, and get rid of it before it is used again.
story: You look after web, the little public website of {{CO}} (made up), on 10.10.22.0/24. Visitors can send photos through an upload form. A colleague thinks something odd was uploaded last night. You have an administrator (root) console on web; the web log is exactly as it was left.
goal: Find the address that uploaded the stray file and the file's name, capture the flag inside it, then delete it and stop the upload folder being writable by every account - before it is used again.
skills: reading a web access log, grep, ls -l, cat, chmod, rm
goalName: use the dropped page against your visitors

shell.WHAT: a tiny web shell: a page that runs commands typed into the address

phish.WHAT: a fake sign-in page that asks visitors for their password

machines.name: web
machines.role: public website (the one you look after)

flags.name: The flag inside the stray file

questions.ask: What address uploaded the stray file?
questions.explain: In the access log this address POSTs to /upload.php late at night and then asks for the new file in /uploads.

questions.ask: What is the stray file's name?
questions.explain: Every other file in /uploads is a .jpg photo; this one isn't.

tasks.name: Stop the uploads folder being writable by every account

attacker.note: The stray file was still there, so it was used again: {{WHAT}}.

hints.text: What to think about first: you are the defender. A web server writes a line to its access log for every page anyone asks for. Somewhere in that log is the moment the stray file arrived. Ask: who uploaded something, what did they upload, and is it still there?

The log is /var/log/httpd/access_log. Each line starts with the visitor's address, then the time, then the request (GET means 'show me a page', POST means 'here is something to save'). cat shows the whole file; grep uploads /var/log/httpd/access_log shows only the lines that mention the uploads folder.

Look at what is in the folder: ls -l /var/www/html/uploads lists it with details (-l). The visitors' photos all end in .jpg; one file doesn't. The address that POSTed to /upload.php just before asking for that file is the uploader. Read the file with cat: the flag is inside.

In the same ls -l line for the folder itself (ls -ld /var/www/html/uploads), drwxrwxrwx means every account on the server may write there - the last rwx is 'everyone else'. chmod 755 /var/www/html/uploads makes it rwxr-xr-x: only the owner can write.

Clean up: rm -f /var/www/html/uploads/{{FILE}} deletes the stray file, and chmod 755 /var/www/html/uploads closes the folder. Then press Check on each fix. (In real life the upload form should also accept only real pictures and never let uploaded files run as pages.)
